prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Long, The, Train

outputs.L1:
Long before you see the train, the tracks sing and tremble. Long before you know the direction from which the train is coming, a hum announces its imminent arrival. So we tend to drop on all fours even before we look left or right. We skip across the sleepers or walk alongside by balancing on a rail. We talk about the capital, where the train ends its run, coming from the interior stacked with the outsized trunks of felled trees and open-topped cars of bauxite.

We always hide from it, unsure what the train will do if we stand next to the tracks. It flattens our nails into knives; it obliterates any traffic caught by it at crossroads. It whistles a battle cry, steam from the engine carrying a mood not to be trifled with. Rails without beginning or end, twinned hopes always at your back, always up front signaling you on: double oxen, hoof-stomp, temper tantrum, stampede, clatter matter, head splitter—hear us, stooped with an ear to the line: greenheart, mora, baromalli, purpleheart, crabwood, kabakalli, womara.
outputs.L2:
Well before the train comes into view,  
the rails begin to quiver and make their music.  
Long before anyone can tell  
which way the train is approaching from,  
a low vibration warns that it is near.

That is why we usually crouch down  
on hands and knees  
before even checking to the left or the right.  
We hop across the wooden sleepers,  
or move beside the track,  
trying to keep our balance along one rail.

We speak of the capital city,  
the place where the train’s journey finishes,  
while its cars come from inland,  
piled high with enormous logs  
from trees that have been cut down,  
and with uncovered wagons full of bauxite.

We never know what it might do  
if we stand too close to the line,  
so we always conceal ourselves from it.  
It can press our nails flat and sharp as blades.  
It can destroy whatever traffic  
it meets at a crossing.  
Its whistle sounds like a war shout,  
and the steam rising from the engine  
carries a warning: do not challenge it.

The rails seem to stretch without origin or ending,  
paired lines of promise behind you,  
paired signs ahead pulling you forward—  
two yoked oxen, hooves pounding,  
rage breaking loose, a stampede,  
noise becoming substance,  
a force that splits the head.  
Listen to us,  
bent low with one ear pressed to the track:  
greenheart, mora, baromalli, purpleheart,  
crabwood, kabakalli, womara.
outputs.L3:
Before the train appears, its presence is felt in the landscape. The first signs are not visual but physical and auditory: a faint trembling runs through the tracks, and a low, distant hum begins to gather in the air. Long before the engine comes into view, the rails themselves seem to announce its approach, carrying the vibration forward like a warning.

The speakers move carefully around the railway line, aware of the danger it represents. They drop low to the ground, balance on the rails, and shift their bodies cautiously as they listen and watch. When the train draws near, they hide from it, treating it almost like a living force that must be respected and avoided. Their movements suggest both curiosity and fear, as they are drawn to the railway but know they must keep themselves safe.

The train is also linked to travel and to the wider world beyond the immediate setting. It suggests journeys to the capital, connecting rural spaces with the centre of power and activity. At the same time, it carries the products of the interior: felled trees, bauxite, and other materials taken from the land. In this way, the train becomes a symbol of movement, trade, extraction, and the connection between the landscape and distant places.

Its power is presented as immense and threatening. The train is capable of smashing through traffic, flattening nails placed on the track, and overwhelming everything in its path. Its sound is compared to a battle cry, making it seem violent, unstoppable, and almost warlike. This imagery emphasizes the danger of the train and the awe it inspires in those who encounter it.

Together, the rails and the train evoke a sense of relentless motion and force. They cut through the landscape while also linking different parts of it, from the forests and interior regions to the city. The presence of felled trees and heavy cargo connects the train to the natural world, especially to the trees that have been removed and transported. As a result, the railway becomes more than a means of transport: it represents power, movement, danger, and the deep relationship between human industry and the land.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the train and its tracks as a powerful, frightening presence that dominates both the landscape and the speaker’s memory. Through vivid sensory imagery, the reader is made to feel the physical force of the train: its noise, vibration, speed, and weight. The tracks are not simply part of the background; they become a place of danger, a boundary that must be approached carefully. The poem’s attention to sound helps recreate the experience of hearing a train before or as it appears, making its arrival feel overwhelming and unavoidable.

The perspective of childhood is central to the poem’s effect. Seen through a child’s eyes, the train seems larger, louder, and more mysterious than an ordinary machine. Its movement inspires fear and fascination at the same time. The child understands that the tracks are dangerous, but also feels drawn to them because they represent motion, distance, and the unknown. This mixture of curiosity and caution gives the poem emotional depth, showing how early experiences of danger can remain vivid in memory.

The poem’s rhythm and sound patterns also contribute to its meaning. Its language often seems to imitate the movement of the train itself, using repeated sounds, heavy beats, or driving rhythms to suggest wheels striking rails. This sound-driven quality makes the train feel present in the poem, not merely described but almost heard and felt. The form of the poem therefore mirrors its subject, turning language into an echo of industrial motion.

At the same time, the train is more than a frightening machine. It also symbolizes extraction, labor, and movement across the land. Trains often carry goods, resources, and people, linking distant places while also reshaping the environments they cross. In this way, the poem suggests that industrial power leaves marks not only on the physical landscape but also on human memory and behavior. The tracks teach people to be careful; the train teaches them to respect force, speed, and danger.

Overall, the poem portrays the train as both a real threat and a larger symbol of industrial power. Its sensory imagery, childhood viewpoint, and rhythmic language combine to show how deeply such a presence can affect the imagination. The train becomes a force that moves through the world with authority, shaping the land, awakening fear, and leaving behind lasting memories of caution and awe.
outputs.L5:
**The Long Train**

The long train moved slowly through the quiet countryside, its wheels singing a steady rhythm on the tracks. Morning light spread across the fields, turning the grass gold and making the windows shine like mirrors. Inside, passengers sat with books, coffee, suitcases, and sleepy thoughts, each one traveling toward a different destination.

The train passed small towns, wide rivers, and forests that seemed to stretch forever. At every station, new people stepped aboard while others waved goodbye and disappeared into the crowd. For some, the journey was ordinary. For others, it was the beginning of something new.

As the hours passed, the long train continued forward, carrying stories, dreams, and memories from one place to another. It reminded everyone that life itself is a journey: sometimes fast, sometimes slow, but always moving ahead.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the voice of a child living near a railway in Guyana, with vivid sensory details about trains carrying timber and bauxite, ending with a list of local hardwood trees.
counterfactuals.output:
At night the train comes  
like thunder learning to walk.

I know it before I see it—  
the rails begin to sing  
under the grass,  
a thin silver shiver  
running past our yard  
where Granny’s zinc roof  
keeps the moon in pieces.

Then the engine mouth opens,  
black smoke and hot oil,  
diesel breath thick as pepperpot,  
and the whole house trembles  
from floorboard to enamel cup.

I run barefoot to the fence,  
red dust sticking to my toes,  
mosquitoes whining round my ears,  
and watch the wagons clank by  
one by one by one,  
loaded with timber—  
big brown logs smelling of rain,  
sap, river mud,  
and deep forest shade.

Some nights it carries bauxite,  
red as crushed brick,  
red as mama’s curry pot,  
red as the road after dry season.  
The powder lifts in the wind  
and settles on our clothesline,  
on the hibiscus leaves,  
on my little brother’s sleeping cheek  
like a secret from the earth.

The train does not wave,  
but I wave anyway.

I think of the men  
far away in the bush,  
their boots wet with creek water,  
their hands bright with sawdust,  
their voices small beneath the trees.  
I think of the mines  
where the ground is opened  
and the red belly of Guyana  
is scooped into iron carts  
to roll past my house  
while frogs sing in the trench  
and the kokers smell of salt and green weeds.

When the last wagon passes,  
the night closes back up.

Only the rails keep humming,  
soft-soft,  
like they are remembering  
every forest,  
every hill,  
every red road home.

Greenheart,  
purpleheart,  
mora,  
crabwood,  
wallaba,  
kabukalli,  
bulletwood,  
silverballi,  
wamara,  
shibadan.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary poem about hearing a train before seeing it, balancing on rails, hiding from its power, and imagining its destination in the capital; use a Caribbean/Guyanese setting and include names like greenheart, mora, baromalli, purpleheart, crabwood, kabakalli, and womara.
counterfactuals.output:
Before the train shows itself,  
it arrives as rumor—  

a tremble in the rusted line,  
a coin of thunder rolling  
under the red dirt road,  
past cane fields gone half-wild,  
past drains glittering with sky.  

We put our ears to the iron  
like children listening for a heartbeat,  
then stand and balance—  
one foot before the other—  
on rails hot with Guyana sun,  
arms wide as if the whole afternoon  
could be crossed this way.  

Greenheart, mora, baromalli,  
purpleheart, crabwood, kabakalli,  
womara—  
the names of trees come up in us  
like old passwords,  
like the forest speaking through sleepers  
and bridges, through every wooden tie  
holding the track in place.  

Then the horn—  
not close, not yet,  
but big enough to change the air.  

We jump down laughing,  
then scatter into bush,  
behind razor grass and fat-leaf bush,  
hiding from the power  
we were daring a minute before.  

The train is still invisible,  
but already it owns the bend,  
the trench, the kiskadee’s cry,  
the whole village holding breath.  

I imagine it going all the way  
to the capital—  
to Georgetown’s seawall,  
to Stabroek’s clock and market roar,  
to minibuses coughing blue smoke,  
to the Demerara widening  
like a thought no one can finish.  

I imagine the carriages full  
of plantain, school uniforms,  
rum-shop arguments,  
a woman with gold bangles asleep  
against the window,  
a boy carrying his first pair of city shoes.  

And still we wait  
in the green heat,  
hidden and listening,  
until the train breaks open  
from behind the trees—  

iron body, black breath,  
future dragging its long noise  
toward us,  
then past us,  
then away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, slightly ominous poem about railway tracks that seem endless, a train loaded with felled trees and bauxite, and children who fear and worship its force.
counterfactuals.output:
The tracks go on where the marsh-light fails,  
two black sutures through the grass,  
stitching the dusk to a farther dusk  
no footstep ever has.

At evening the red train comes,  
dragging the hill’s broken bones—  
felled trees, sap still dark with weather,  
bauxite burning like buried coals.

Its iron lungs pull hard at the town,  
its wheels preach thunder to the stones;  
every coupling clanks like a chain  
in a god’s enormous throat.

Children gather by the weeds  
with bottle caps and solemn eyes,  
half in terror, half in prayer,  
as the engine shoulders by.

They know its hunger, know its heat,  
the way it makes the sleepers shake,  
the way the sky itself seems split  
beneath the whistle’s blade.

And when it passes, long and long,  
into the country no one names,  
the rails keep humming after dark—  
two endless lines of flame.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an imagistic poem with no title about the approach of a train: the trembling tracks, the whistle, steam, crushed objects, and the speaker placing an ear to the rail; make the language dense, rhythmic, and rooted in Guyanese landscape.
counterfactuals.output:
I lay my ear to the iron—  
hot vein through cane-field,  
through koker-mouth, trench-water,  
through mud where crabs stitch sideways  
and the punt-rope sags with rain.

A tremor first:  
not sound, but a black ant-worry  
under the rail,  
a tin-cup shiver,  
a spoon in the enamel basin  
beginning its small obeah dance.

Far off, the whistle—  
long white cutlass of breath  
slashing the afternoon’s green throat.  
Egrets lift like torn cloth  
from the rice flats;  
a dog stops barking  
with foam on its teeth.

Then steam—  
cassava-smoke, bagasse-smoke,  
cloud dragged low from the Demerara,  
salt and coal and hot grease  
rolling over the village roofs,  
over zinc, over breadfruit leaf,  
over old women’s wash  
snapping bright as fish.

The track trembles harder.  
Bolts sweat.  
Sleepers groan in their black oil.  
In the dust beside the line:  
a mango skinned to yellow bruise,  
a bottle-cap flattened into moon,  
cane-frog, dragonfly,  
the red hibiscus crushed  
to a wet tongue.

I keep my ear there—  
fool-child, river-child—  
hearing the engine before the engine:  
iron rain, iron hoof,  
all Georgetown thunder  
coming inland, coming,  
coming with its furnace belly,  
its brass throat calling,  
its wheels beating  
Demerara, Berbice, Essequibo—  
one dark drum under the ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a free verse poem inspired by colonial railways and resource extraction in the interior, where the train becomes an animal-like force—oxen, stampede, battle cry—and include references to timber species at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
The rail was laid like a command  
across the inland’s breathing back,  
iron stitched into red earth,  
sleepers pressed down  
where roots once held the dark together.

From the coast came surveyors,  
maps folded like orders,  
their pencils sharpening valleys  
into routes of removal.

Then the train arrived—  
not a machine, not only—  
but a yoke of black oxen  
snorting coal smoke,  
shoulders heaving steam,  
dragging the interior behind it.

It bellowed through grassland,  
a stampede with one spine,  
wheels hammering the ground  
until villages woke to its battle cry,  
until hills answered  
with echoes of iron.

Carriage by carriage,  
the forest was made portable.  
Rivers were crossed,  
mountains opened,  
ore and sap and grain and bone  
counted, branded, sent away.

At dawn, the engine drank water  
like a war animal at a trough.  
At dusk, it hauled the day’s hunger  
toward the harbor,  
where ships waited with open mouths.

And in the cut interior,  
stumps stood like witnesses,  
rings exposed—  
years translated into cargo,  
shade turned into ledger.

Still, under the ash,  
seeds kept their small rebellions.

Still, the names of trees  
gathered at the edge of the track:

teak, mahogany, iroko, sal,  
cedar, ebony, rosewood,  
greenheart, merbau, camphor,  
sapele, baobab, pine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
